title: Elimination
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: OR11#t3 term and clue written for the game; OR11#t4 term and clue written for the game; OR11#t1 term and clue written for the game; OR11#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: OR11#N.2, OR11#N.5, OR11#N.7, OR11#N.9, OR11#N.11.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Nucleophile
items.clue: Role of OH⁻ when it donates a lone pair to a δ+ carbon atom.

items.label: Base
items.clue: Role of OH⁻ when it accepts H⁺ from the carbon next to the C–Br carbon.

items.label: Elimination
items.clue: A small molecule is removed from two neighbouring carbons, leaving a C=C.

items.label: Substitution
items.clue: Reaction favoured by warm aqueous KOH, turning a halogenoalkane mainly into an alcohol.

questions.stem: 2-bromopropane is heated under reflux with potassium hydroxide dissolved in ethanol, and propene forms. What is the role of the hydroxide ion?

options.text: It is a nucleophile: it donates a lone pair to the carbon bonded to Br.
It is an electrophile: it accepts a pair of electrons from the C–Br bond.
It is a base: it accepts H⁺ from a carbon next to the C–Br carbon.
It is a catalyst: it is given back at the end, so it is written over the arrow.

questions.explanation: OH⁻ takes an H⁺ from the neighbouring carbon and becomes H₂O. Br⁻ leaves, and a C=C forms between the two carbons.

questions.stem: A chemist wants as much propene, and as little propan-2-ol, as possible from 2-bromopropane. Which conditions should be used?

options.text: Aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol, warmed
Potassium hydroxide with ultraviolet light, at room temperature
Potassium hydroxide dissolved in ethanol, heated under reflux

questions.explanation: Ethanol as the solvent and a high temperature favour OH⁻ acting as a base. Some propan-2-ol still forms, as the two reactions compete.

questions.stem: In the mechanism for the elimination of HBr from 2-bromopropane by hydroxide ions, where does the first curly arrow start and finish?

options.text: From the C–Br bond to the Br atom, which leaves as a bromide ion
From an O lone pair of OH⁻ to an H on a carbon next to the C–Br carbon
From a lone pair on the O of OH⁻ to the δ+ carbon atom of the C–Br bond
From the C=C bond to the H atom of a water molecule

questions.explanation: OH⁻ acts as a base, forming an O–H bond. The C–H pair moves to make the C=C bond, and the C–Br pair leaves with Br.

questions.stem: 2-bromo-2-methylbutane, (CH₃)₂CBrCH₂CH₃, is heated with ethanolic potassium hydroxide. How many different alkenes can form?
questions.explanation: H from a CH₃ gives 2-methylbut-1-ene. H from the CH₂ gives 2-methylbut-2-ene. Its C2 carries two CH₃ groups, so it has no E/Z isomers.

questions.stem: Chlorocyclohexane is warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide in one tube, and heated under reflux with sodium hydroxide in ethanol in another. The main product in the second tube is cyclohexene. Which statement explains the second result?

options.text: In ethanol, OH⁻ bonds to the δ+ carbon of the C–Cl bond, and Cl⁻ leaves.
In ethanol, the solvent removes HCl from chlorocyclohexane, and OH⁻ just neutralises the HCl.
In ethanol, OH⁻ mainly acts as a base, removing H⁺ from a carbon next to the C–Cl carbon.
In ethanol, the ring opens as OH⁻ breaks a C–C bond, and a gaseous product is released.
